title: Factors for Successful Reviews
concept:
Reviews can fail to deliver value despite ticking all the procedural boxes. CTFL lists factors that distinguish effective reviews.

**Clear objectives** — every review should have a stated objective (find defects? build consensus? transfer knowledge?). The objectives shape the technique, the participants, and the success criteria.

**Right people** — reviewers chosen for relevant skills and perspectives. Too few or too narrow a set misses defects.

**Appropriate technique** — chosen to match the objective and the work product. A safety-critical requirements review uses inspection with checklists; a sprint code review uses informal review with a perspective focus.

**Pre-review preparation** — reviewers read the work product *before* the meeting; the meeting is for discussion, not first exposure.

**Manageable scope** — small enough to review thoroughly. Splitting a large work product into smaller chunks dramatically improves defect detection.

**Defects, not solutions** — the review identifies defects; the author fixes them after. Trying to resolve every defect in the meeting wastes time and pulls the meeting off-track.

**Author-friendly culture** — comments target the work product, not the author. Defects are normal.

**Follow-up** — defects are logged, tracked, and verified as resolved. Without follow-up, reviews become theatre.
keyPoints: Success factors: clear objectives, right people, appropriate technique, preparation, manageable scope, defect-focus, supportive culture, follow-up.
Reviewers must prepare *before* the meeting; live first-reads waste everyone's time.
The review identifies defects; the author fixes them after — don't solve every defect live.

quiz.question: A team holds 2-hour reviews of a 100-page design document and finds few defects. Which adjustment is MOST likely to improve effectiveness?
options: Split the document into smaller chunks and review each separately with prepared reviewers.
Skip the review and rely on dynamic testing.
Have the author present the full document at the meeting.
quiz.explanation: Manageable scope is a key success factor. Splitting a large document into chunks lets reviewers prepare thoroughly and concentrate on each part — far more effective than fatiguing through 100 pages in one meeting. Skipping reviews loses early-defect-detection value; having the author present forfeits independent perspective.
